summary: Gives instructions to IANA for creating a new registry of codepoints for the flags field in the Session Attribute object of RSVP-TE signaling messages. These are used in MPLS and Generalized MPLS. It is an informational document.

eli5.summary: Flags in a message are like switches on a control panel. This note asks the keeper of the lists to start a master list of what each switch means, so nobody reuses one by accident.

questions: what are rsvp-te session attribute flags
how to request a new rsvp-te flag
subtitle: A registry for the flag bits in RSVP-TE session messages

tldr.problem: RSVP-TE (Resource Reservation Protocol for Traffic Engineering) includes an 8-bit flags field in its Session Attribute object. As MPLS and GMPLS protocols evolved, different RFCs assigned uses to different bits, with no central registry to prevent conflicts.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4859 lists the existing bit assignments from earlier RFCs and asks IANA to create a new codepoint registry to track which bits mean what, ensuring no bit is assigned twice and defining clear procedures for future assignments.
tldr.outcome: A formal registry prevents bit conflicts and makes it clear how engineers should request new bits. IETF consensus is required to assign new flags.

today: RFC 4859 is Informational and established the registry that IANA maintains. The Session Attribute Object Flags registry is part of the official RSVP-TE Parameters registries and is still used today when new MPLS and GMPLS features need to be added.

sections.title: The Problem and the Solution
sections.content:
RSVP-TE is used to set up label-switched paths (LSPs) in MPLS and GMPLS networks. It extends the original RSVP with traffic engineering features. The Session Attribute object in an RSVP-TE Path message carries an 8-bit field of flags, where each bit can mean "yes, please do this" for a particular feature.

RFC 3209 defined three of these bits. Later, RFC 4090 added two more, and RFC 4736 added one more. Without a registry, the next RFC writer might not know which bits were already used, and accidentally reuse a bit for something different. RFC 4859 solves this by asking IANA to create and manage the registry.
sections.eli5: The message has eight lights, and different engineers had been turning on different lights for different reasons. This note says let's make an official list so nobody gets confused.

sections.title: What the Bits Mean Today
sections.content:
From RFC 3209: bit 0x01 means "local protection desired", 0x02 means "label recording desired", 0x04 means "SE Style desired". From RFC 4090: 0x08 means "bandwidth protection desired", 0x10 means "node protection desired". From RFC 4736: 0x20 means "path re-evaluation request".

This gives IANA a starting list. Future RFCs can request new bits from the unassigned ones (0x40, 0x80, etc.).
sections.eli5: Some bits already mean: protect along a backup route, record the labels, protect bandwidth, protect nodes, and ask for a fresh calculation of the best route.

sections.title: How New Flags Are Assigned
sections.content:
New flags can only be assigned through IETF consensus, as defined in RFC 2434. This high bar ensures that every new feature gets careful review from the Internet engineering community before a bit is permanently allocated to it.

The registry is placed under the "RSVP-TE Parameters" branch in IANA's tree of registries. Anyone who needs a new flag must make a case to the IETF that it is necessary and well-designed.
sections.eli5: If someone needs to turn on a new light, they have to convince the whole Internet engineering community that it's a good idea, so we don't run out of lights for silly reasons.
